Share on X Telegram The Edo State Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC), Obo Effanga on Friday, said that the state currently has 2.8 million registered voters. He said the last registration exercise raised the figure, noting that the final figure would be released after the recent clean up exercise by the national body. INEC had earlier said a total number of 131,165 new voters were registered in the just concluded Continuous Voter Registration exercise, which took place between August 2025 and July 2026. Giving an update on the Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) collection, Effanga said a total of 23,401 cards had been collected across the state since distribution commenced on October 9. Ettanga explained that the figure comprised 6,319 old PVCs, 5,128 newly produced cards and 11,954 PVCs relating to transfers. Effanga noted, “The state currently has 2.8 million registered voters after the last registration exercise. However, the final figure would be released after the recent clean up exercise by the national body.” The REC disclosed that PVCs for voters who registered during the first and second phases of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise were currently available for collection at INEC offices across the 18 local government areas of the state. He recalled that the first phase of the registration exercise lasted from August to December 2025, while the second phase took place between January and April 2026. The resident commissioner said the commission was currently working towards ensuring a smooth electoral process. Speaking on the mock accreditation exercise scheduled for November 28, the REC said the exercise would be conducted in 384 polling units across the state. He explained that Edo State had 192 registration areas, also known as wards, with two polling units selected from each registration area for the exercise. “The exercise would provide an opportunity to test the commission’s electoral technology and assess the readiness of its personnel ahead of the elections. “The state office had submitted the list of proposed polling units to the commission’s headquarters for approval,” he added. He said the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System would be deployed during the exercise to demonstrate how voters are accredited, how results are captured and how they are transmitted to the INEC Result Viewing Portal. The REC explained that INEC does not have sufficient permanent staff to conduct elections across the state’s 4,519 polling units, making the recruitment of ad hoc personnel necessary. He stressed that recruitment would commence after the closure of the application portal, when the commission’s headquarters would process applicants’ details and forward the names to the respective states based on their preferred locations of service. He added that successful applicants would subsequently be invited for screening and training before deployment. The REC identified supervisory presiding officers and collation officers as other categories of ad hoc personnel. He explained that supervisory presiding officers were usually selected from among senior civil servants, particularly federal civil servants who met the required grade-level qualifications. Responding to concerns over the safety of ad hoc staff, particularly in view of previous incidents of violence during elections, the REC said INEC was working with security agencies to ensure adequate protection for everyone involved in the electoral process. He emphasised that security arrangements would cover not only election officials but also voters, journalists and other stakeholders participating in the exercise. According to him, the commission has been holding regular meetings of the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security, with the latest meeting held on Tuesday. He disclosed that he will also participate in a national summit on election security organised by the Office of the National Security Adviser in collaboration with INEC. The REC, however, noted that maintaining electoral security required the cooperation of all stakeholders, particularly politicians, whom he accused of sometimes encouraging violence through their actions and campaign rhetoric. He said politicians must understand that elections were civil exercises and should not threaten or intimidate voters into supporting particular candidates. He condemned statements suggesting that people who refused to vote for certain candidates should not visit particular communities, describing such rhetoric as unacceptable. On whether election personnel were covered by insurance in the event of injuries or other incidents during elections, the REC confirmed that the commission had insurance arrangements for those engaged in the electoral process. He said the insurance included life coverage and explained that INEC had previously taken responsibility for medical treatment and other necessary support for corps members injured while performing electoral duties.
